title: The weekend is 100 years old – but have ‘skiveday Fridays’ and hybrid working ruined it for everyone?
excerpt: In 1926, Henry Ford gave his employees both Saturdays and Sundays off – and the two-day chunk of time to party, pray or simply do nothing was born. Now it’s changed beyond recognition
content_html:
For 11 years, from 1929 to 1940, the Soviet Union did not have weekends. Instead, to increase productivity citizens were allocated a day off in every seven at random. With 80% of the population at work on any given day, factories never had to power down.

A letter from a disgruntled worker to Pravda newspaper, published soon after the implementation of this new working calendar, outlined the problems: “What is there for us to do at home if our wives are in the factory, our children at school, and nobody can visit us?” the letter-writer asked. “It is no holiday if you have to have it alone.” Parents found themselves at home while their children were at school, or with kids unsupervised while they were on shift. With no shared day off, extended family gatherings became impossible. The workforce became demoralised and listless, the projected spike in productivity never materialised, and the policy was first modified, then abandoned altogether.

Eleven years, though. Is that not absolutely wild? A world without weekends feels impossible. A world without Saturday Night Fever, without Manic Monday. We may no longer go to church on Sunday, but we still worship the weekend. “The weekend looms large because it represents the triumph of collective time over market time,” says Brad Beaven, professor of social and cultural history at the University of Portsmouth. “It is not just about rest, but about reclaiming autonomy from the industrial clock.”

Saturday and Sunday, sacred to the dignity and humanity of working people, are laden with mythology and ceremony. From Cilla Black to Gary Lineker, the main characters of our weekends become giants of the culture. We romanticise the weekend, even the prosaic bits – the distant roar of a lawnmower, the rattle of classified football results on the radio. Everyone knows what a weekend means. The snap of a laptop cover at 4.58pm on a Friday. The clink of the first pint glass and the smell of chips on the way home. The slow-motion pace of a weekend pavement, the gear change from hustle to meander. The rituals have changed with the times, of course, and people-watching at brunch on Saturday is now as much of a tradition as cooking a roast at home on Sunday. A weekend changes shape as you move through life stages, but in each iteration it remains a shared experience between you and your peers.

“The weekend that I had when I was 20 was very different from the weekend that I have now, at 40 and with kids,” laughs Pedro Gomes, professor of economics at Birkbeck, University of London and author of the book Friday is the New Saturday. “When you are young, you are bonding with your friends, and then when you get older, you might be with your family. Eventually, you might be with grandchildren. We move through different manifestations of the weekend, in our lifetimes.”

But it can be hard to pin down, these days, where a weekend begins and ends. Laundry gets done on a work-from-home Friday, but emails are answered on Sunday. A shopping splurge is as likely to be a cheer-up treat on your phone after a tough Wednesday as a Saturday outing. The traditional Saturday 3pm football kick-off has been stretched across the television schedules all the way to Monday evening. The four-day week – first predicted by Richard Nixon, of all people, in 1956 – has become a reality in the Netherlands, with people working an average of 32.1 hours. Friday is forging ahead with a quiet secession from the working week without anyone signing off the paperwork. It raises the question: what even is “the weekend” in 2026?

Remarkably, the concept of the weekend as we know it is only 100 years old. In 1926, Henry Ford changed the shape of the week, announcing that the workers at his factories would now do five eight-hour days instead of six, with no cut in pay. Ford did not invent the weekend – the idea had been bubbling under for a century, in campaigns by trade unions, religious groups and progressive employers – but by putting his considerable industrial weight behind it, the two-day chunk of freedom was born.

“It is high time to rid ourselves of the notion that leisure for workmen is either lost time or a class privilege,” Ford wrote in his company’s Ford News in October 1926. Ford’s innovation was in part a response to his earlier invention: the assembly line, which had increased productivity but exhausted workers, with absenteeism up to 10% in factories; in his article he did not disguise that there was self-interest involved. “People who have more leisure require more transportation in vehicles,” he continued. The new fashion for day trips was an effective marketing device to sell cars. Meanwhile, his factories maintained a steady level of productivity despite the reduced hours. In 1938, faced with rising unemployment levels in the Great Depression, the five-day week was officially adopted across the US.

On this side of the Atlantic, Boots the Chemist was the pioneer. In 1933, the company opened a new factory in Nottingham, which proved so efficient that there was soon a surplus of stock. Reluctant to lay his staff off with unemployment running at 25%, John Boot ended the Saturday morning shift, reducing hours for the 5,000-strong workforce without cutting wages. It was commercially successful, resulting in lower rates of absenteeism, and was adopted as Boots policy in 1934. A government inquiry led by Richard Redmayne – great-grandfather, fun fact, of actor Eddie – published a “review of the experimental working of the five days week”, which noted “an improvement in stamina and animation of the employees arising from the physiological and psychological effects of a long weekend’s rest and relaxation”. Slowly, the weekend gathered momentum. In the UK, “the early 20th-century version of the weekend was generally recognised as a half-day Saturday and Sunday off,” says Beaven. “The full two-day weekend only really became widely adopted after the second world war.”

Before industrialisation, there was little concept of consecutive days of leisure, because animals and crops could not be so long neglected. Work was dictated by the weather and the seasons, the clock mattering less than the sun. Factories, with their whistles and watches, changed the way time worked. A mechanised drumbeat of shifts and paydays drowned out the old rhythms of seasons and saints days.

As work became more rigidly organised, the possibility emerged that leisure could be, too. Time off wasn’t merely a concession to workers, but also an engine of consumer capitalism. People with weekends would go to sports stadiums, buy picnic baskets and new clothes, need cinema tickets. By the late 20th century, with the arrival of cheap flights, this had evolved into the minibreak: a miniature holiday, designed to fit into a weekend. Leisure time, once the opposite of the economy, became part of it.

For generations, the British weekend revolved around one immovable appointment: the 3pm Saturday kick-off. “The weekend is about rest, but it is also about passion,” says Gomes. “Most of us are not lucky enough to be passionate about our jobs, but at the weekend we can follow our passions.” The link between football and the best day of the week is intrinsic to the national love affair with the sport. It is probably partly because football symbolised the best bit of the weekend that we ended up so obsessed with it.

Morals – and the absence of them – have always been a theme of the weekend. When Sunday, a time of worship, was the only day off, skilled workers developed a habit of extending their free time into “Saint Monday”, by not turning up for work after a particularly enthusiastic day of drinking. Saturday afternoons off – and then the whole day – were granted by employers partly in the hope of bringing the hangovers forward by a day. Victorian reformers, obsessed with drunkenness, hoped that free Saturdays would encourage respectable recreation: organised sport, gardening, family outings. Ford, a vehement supporter of Prohibition, believed that the illegality of alcohol made his move towards a two-day weekend safe. (“A day off is no longer a day drunk,” he said.)

The reality has never been quite so clean-cut. Weekends are naughty and nice, both bad behaviour and Sunday best. These are the days for shopping splurges and drinking sprees and hook-ups, but also for penance, whether by parkrun, DIY or actual prayer. Though perhaps less so the prayer bit: around one in three Britons attended church regularly in 1900, according to the National Centre for Social Research; now, this is number is around one in 20. Two moments stand out in the story of how Sunday lost its special place as a day, if not of worship, then of higher purpose. In 1994, the Sunday Trading Act allowed large shops in England and Wales to open on Sundays. Then, a quarter of a century later, pandemic lockdowns broke the now-fragile bonds between churches and their communities, and left many older parishioners with a wariness of gathering in ill-ventilated churches that might be bad for the health, even if good for the soul.

The late, great Maggie Smith had, as she so often did, the best line. “What is a weekend?” she asked, in Downton Abbey, with the entitled bewilderment of a dowager countess for whom income is spoonfed in silver from birth, not doled out in a brown envelope on a Friday night. The weekend is time carved out of, and in tension with, someone else’s ownership of your time. Not to mention that for aristocrats, who had servants for everything from laying fires to buttoning their dresses, every day was a day of leisure. The weekend feels like a cornerstone of civilisation, of democracy, because it matters most to those who spend the majority of the week following orders instead of giving them.

These days, the upstairs-downstairs division is between the hybrid workers and those whose work can never be done remotely. An age-old division between shift work and the relative flexibility of white-collar jobs has deepened. Thinkers like Liselotte Lyngsø, founding partner of the Copenhagen-based consultancy Future Navigator, have argued that the workforce is splitting into “time owners” – knowledge workers who increasingly choose where and when they work – and “time slaves”, whose jobs, like healthcare, manual shift work or gig economy roles like Amazon or Deliveroo driving, remains stubbornly tied to the clock.

For the “time owners”, Friday is rapidly turning into the modern Saint Monday. It is an increasingly open secret that the last day of the working week has become, for remote workers, an unofficial half shift: calendar technically open, but both brain and laptop mostly on standby. When Gomes ran a six-month trial of four-day-week working in Portugal in 2023, with more than 41 public and private firms involved, “organisations that can’t reduce hours – a nursery, for example – worked in shifts with a different day off within each week. Other firms made the decision to cut Friday out. Whenever their weekday off was, we found that many employees approached that day a little differently, using it to get ‘life admin’ done so that they could have their Saturdays and Sundays free. The weekend isn’t just about the number of hours, it is also a coordination device for communities to connect.”

As with Saint Monday, “Skiveday Friday” has proved in the UK to be stubbornly, if silently, adhered to. In 2024, Transport for London ran a three-month trial scrapping peak fares on Fridays explicitly in order to lure commuters back into central London. It failed, Fridays remaining quiet, despite the discount. For the laptopped-classes, there has been a shift in what Friday is for. Several major rail companies, including LNER and Avanti, have now made Fridays an entirely off-peak day like Saturday and Sunday, acknowledging that the weekend now begins earlier for many.

Though it should be noted that, for those same workers, Saturday and Sunday themselves are under constant siege from the mission creep of work emails and contactability outside working hours in the age of the smartphone. “These are two sides of the same coin,” says Gomes. Work intensifies, and the weekend expands in order to absorb the pressure. “The speed of communication means that we now live with constant interruptions, and it is hard to find space either for deep work or for real rest. And yet we continue to structure the work week in much the same way as we did 100 years ago. It is no surprise that this isn’t working.”

Hence why a three-day weekend is being suggested as a way to balance the books. But is it all woke nonsense? A pie in the sky idea, dreamed up by a lazy workforce which no longer knows the meaning of hard work? The Green party supports a “move towards” a four-day week, but other politicians are wary. In 2025, the Liberal Democrat-led South Cambridgeshire council, which had been operating a four-day week for two years, was attacked by the then local government secretary, Steve Reed, who said that local governments “should not be paying full-time wages for part-time work”. In April this year, James Cleverly announced that a future Conservative government would look to ban four-day weeks for council staff, denouncing the “push from the left of centre in British politics” towards a four-day week as “completely wrong”.

The 4 Day Week Foundation, which is leading the drive for change in Britain, says that 56 out of the 61 companies who signed up for their four-day week pilot decided to stick with it after the scheme ended. They cite an average of 35% increased revenue, and 57% decline in staff leaving rates, during the trial. There are now 260 companies in the UK officially signed up to the four-day week.

The divide – between time sharers and time slaves, those working five-day weeks, four-day weeks or more ad-hoc, less weekend-friendly shift work – is problematic because the weekend is designed to be shared. It’s where British culture learned to gather, a collective experience. Every generation has its own shared rituals. Boomers love a Saturday night movie, generation X are obsessed with Sunday lunch, millennials love to flock to a farmers’ market, while gen Z, for some reason, get their kicks standing in line for baked goods that have gone viral on TikTok. Even the Sunday scaries are made manageable by the knowledge that everyone out there is feeling the same. As a gulf widens – between the time owners and time slaves, between inherited wealth and the increasingly weedy salary pipeline – the weekend starts to feel less like an experience, and more like a nostalgic memory.

It is funny to think that, at first, technology expanded our horizons. Railways gave ordinary people access to the coast; mass production made bicycles and cars affordable. It is only recently that technology has mutated into the energy vampire it is today, sucking the life from the weekend.

Only in the last decade has online autobiography become everybody’s unpaid side hustle, so that your friends have already seen your holiday photos before you meet them for brunch. It is a very modern phenomenon that our friendships have migrated online, this week’s boy drama or family quarrel already debated at length in text bubbles and voice notes without the need to meet in the pub. Add to this the post-pandemic normalisation of the “soft commitment”, in which making plans and cancelling them have become two parts of the same social ritual and “I’ll see how I feel” has become an acceptable RSVP, and we have become less good at a core element of the weekend, which is actually seeing other people.

Perhaps we shouldn’t fret so much. Ever since we invented the weekend, we have been anxiously taking its pulse. The Victorians worried that workers would waste their precious leisure days drinking. Mid-century Britain feared television was keeping families indoors. Today’s concern is that we spend Saturday scrolling Instagram and Sunday answering emails. The rituals change; the suspicion that the weekend is being ruined remains. Yet the weekend survives, perhaps because it has never demanded perfection. The lie-in and the late night are equally valid forms of resistance. Its holiest rites – the greasy fry-up, the football terrace, Saturday-night shiny-floor television – are gloriously unrefined. The weekend is where a good time still trumps good taste.

The Soviets discovered that a day off is not much use unless other people are off, too; Ford understood that workers needed time in which to become themselves again, even if he hoped they would spend it buying cars. At 100, the two-day weekend is fraying at the edges, leaking into Friday and nibbled away by Sunday night emails. The weekend will keep changing, because work keeps changing. But it will still always be the best thing work ever invented.

blocks.html_en: Saturday and Sunday, sacred to the dignity and humanity of working people, are laden with mythology and ceremony. From Cilla Black to Gary Lineker, the main characters of our weekends become giants of the culture. We romanticise the weekend, even the prosaic bits – the distant roar of a lawnmower, the rattle of classified football results on the radio. Everyone knows what a weekend means. The snap of a laptop cover at 4.58pm on a Friday. The clink of the first pint glass and the smell of chips on the way home. The slow-motion pace of a weekend pavement, the gear change from hustle to meander. The rituals have changed with the times, of course, and people-watching at brunch on Saturday is now as much of a tradition as cooking a roast at home on Sunday. A weekend changes shape as you move through life stages, but in each iteration it remains a shared experience between you and your peers.

blocks.html_en: “The weekend that I had when I was 20 was very different from the weekend that I have now, at 40 and with kids,” laughs Pedro Gomes, professor of economics at Birkbeck, University of London and author of the book Friday is the New Saturday. “When you are young, you are bonding with your friends, and then when you get older, you might be with your family. Eventually, you might be with grandchildren. We move through different manifestations of the weekend, in our lifetimes.”

blocks.html_en: But it can be hard to pin down, these days, where a weekend begins and ends. Laundry gets done on a work-from-home Friday, but emails are answered on Sunday. A shopping splurge is as likely to be a cheer-up treat on your phone after a tough Wednesday as a Saturday outing. The traditional Saturday 3pm football kick-off has been stretched across the television schedules all the way to Monday evening. The four-day week – first predicted by Richard Nixon, of all people, in 1956 – has become a reality in the Netherlands, with people working an average of 32.1 hours. Friday is forging ahead with a quiet secession from the working week without anyone signing off the paperwork. It raises the question: what even is “the weekend” in 2026?

blocks.html_en: Remarkably, the concept of the weekend as we know it is only 100 years old. In 1926, Henry Ford changed the shape of the week, announcing that the workers at his factories would now do five eight-hour days instead of six, with no cut in pay. Ford did not invent the weekend – the idea had been bubbling under for a century, in campaigns by trade unions, religious groups and progressive employers – but by putting his considerable industrial weight behind it, the two-day chunk of freedom was born.

sentences.en: In 1926, Henry Ford changed the shape of the week, announcing that the workers at his factories would now do five eight-hour days instead of six, with no cut in pay.

blocks.html_en: “It is high time to rid ourselves of the notion that leisure for workmen is either lost time or a class privilege,” Ford wrote in his company’s Ford News in October 1926. Ford’s innovation was in part a response to his earlier invention: the assembly line, which had increased productivity but exhausted workers, with absenteeism up to 10% in factories; in his article he did not disguise that there was self-interest involved. “People who have more leisure require more transportation in vehicles,” he continued. The new fashion for day trips was an effective marketing device to sell cars. Meanwhile, his factories maintained a steady level of productivity despite the reduced hours. In 1938, faced with rising unemployment levels in the Great Depression, the five-day week was officially adopted across the US.

blocks.html_en: On this side of the Atlantic, Boots the Chemist was the pioneer. In 1933, the company opened a new factory in Nottingham, which proved so efficient that there was soon a surplus of stock. Reluctant to lay his staff off with unemployment running at 25%, John Boot ended the Saturday morning shift, reducing hours for the 5,000-strong workforce without cutting wages. It was commercially successful, resulting in lower rates of absenteeism, and was adopted as Boots policy in 1934. A government inquiry led by Richard Redmayne – great-grandfather, fun fact, of actor Eddie – published a “review of the experimental working of the five days week”, which noted “an improvement in stamina and animation of the employees arising from the physiological and psychological effects of a long weekend’s rest and relaxation”. Slowly, the weekend gathered momentum. In the UK, “the early 20th-century version of the weekend was generally recognised as a half-day Saturday and Sunday off,” says Beaven. “The full two-day weekend only really became widely adopted after the second world war.”

blocks.html_en: Before industrialisation, there was little concept of consecutive days of leisure, because animals and crops could not be so long neglected. Work was dictated by the weather and the seasons, the clock mattering less than the sun. Factories, with their whistles and watches, changed the way time worked. A mechanised drumbeat of shifts and paydays drowned out the old rhythms of seasons and saints days.

blocks.html_en: As work became more rigidly organised, the possibility emerged that leisure could be, too. Time off wasn’t merely a concession to workers, but also an engine of consumer capitalism. People with weekends would go to sports stadiums, buy picnic baskets and new clothes, need cinema tickets. By the late 20th century, with the arrival of cheap flights, this had evolved into the minibreak: a miniature holiday, designed to fit into a weekend. Leisure time, once the opposite of the economy, became part of it.

blocks.html_en: For generations, the British weekend revolved around one immovable appointment: the 3pm Saturday kick-off. “The weekend is about rest, but it is also about passion,” says Gomes. “Most of us are not lucky enough to be passionate about our jobs, but at the weekend we can follow our passions.” The link between football and the best day of the week is intrinsic to the national love affair with the sport. It is probably partly because football symbolised the best bit of the weekend that we ended up so obsessed with it.

blocks.html_en: Morals – and the absence of them – have always been a theme of the weekend. When Sunday, a time of worship, was the only day off, skilled workers developed a habit of extending their free time into “Saint Monday”, by not turning up for work after a particularly enthusiastic day of drinking. Saturday afternoons off – and then the whole day – were granted by employers partly in the hope of bringing the hangovers forward by a day. Victorian reformers, obsessed with drunkenness, hoped that free Saturdays would encourage respectable recreation: organised sport, gardening, family outings. Ford, a vehement supporter of Prohibition, believed that the illegality of alcohol made his move towards a two-day weekend safe. (“A day off is no longer a day drunk,” he said.)

blocks.html_en: The reality has never been quite so clean-cut. Weekends are naughty and nice, both bad behaviour and Sunday best. These are the days for shopping splurges and drinking sprees and hook-ups, but also for penance, whether by parkrun, DIY or actual prayer. Though perhaps less so the prayer bit: around one in three Britons attended church regularly in 1900, according to the National Centre for Social Research; now, this is number is around one in 20. Two moments stand out in the story of how Sunday lost its special place as a day, if not of worship, then of higher purpose. In 1994, the Sunday Trading Act allowed large shops in England and Wales to open on Sundays. Then, a quarter of a century later, pandemic lockdowns broke the now-fragile bonds between churches and their communities, and left many older parishioners with a wariness of gathering in ill-ventilated churches that might be bad for the health, even if good for the soul.

sentences.en: The reality has never been quite so clean-cut.
sentences.zh: 现实从未如此清晰。

blocks.html_en: The late, great Maggie Smith had, as she so often did, the best line. “What is a weekend?” she asked, in Downton Abbey, with the entitled bewilderment of a dowager countess for whom income is spoonfed in silver from birth, not doled out in a brown envelope on a Friday night. Not to mention that for aristocrats, who had servants for everything from laying fires to buttoning their dresses, every day was a day of leisure. The weekend feels like a cornerstone of civilisation, of democracy, because it matters most to those who spend the majority of the week following orders instead of giving them.

blocks.html_en: For the “time owners”, Friday is rapidly turning into the modern Saint Monday. It is an increasingly open secret that the last day of the working week has become, for remote workers, an unofficial half shift: calendar technically open, but both brain and laptop mostly on standby. When Gomes ran a six-month trial of four-day-week working in Portugal in 2023, with more than 41 public and private firms involved, “organisations that can’t reduce hours – a nursery, for example – worked in shifts with a different day off within each week. Other firms made the decision to cut Friday out. Whenever their weekday off was, we found that many employees approached that day a little differently, using it to get ‘life admin’ done so that they could have their Saturdays and Sundays free. The weekend isn’t just about the number of hours, it is also a coordination device for communities to connect.”

blocks.html_en: The divide – between time sharers and time slaves, those working five-day weeks, four-day weeks or more ad-hoc, less weekend-friendly shift work – is problematic because the weekend is designed to be shared. It’s where British culture learned to gather, a collective experience. Every generation has its own shared rituals. Boomers love a Saturday night movie, generation X are obsessed with Sunday lunch, millennials love to flock to a farmers’ market, while gen Z, for some reason, get their kicks standing in line for baked goods that have gone viral on TikTok. Even the Sunday scaries are made manageable by the knowledge that everyone out there is feeling the same. As a gulf widens – between the time owners and time slaves, between inherited wealth and the increasingly weedy salary pipeline – the weekend starts to feel less like an experience, and more like a nostalgic memory.

blocks.html_en: Perhaps we shouldn’t fret so much. Ever since we invented the weekend, we have been anxiously taking its pulse. The Victorians worried that workers would waste their precious leisure days drinking. Mid-century Britain feared television was keeping families indoors. Today’s concern is that we spend Saturday scrolling Instagram and Sunday answering emails. The rituals change; the suspicion that the weekend is being ruined remains. Yet the weekend survives, perhaps because it has never demanded perfection. The lie-in and the late night are equally valid forms of resistance. Its holiest rites – the greasy fry-up, the football terrace, Saturday-night shiny-floor television – are gloriously unrefined. The weekend is where a good time still trumps good taste.

sentences.zh: 苏联人发现，除非其他人也休息，否则休息一天并没有多大用处。福特明白，工人们需要时间来重新做回自己，即使他希望他们用这段时间购买汽车。

content_html_zh:
从1929年到1940年，苏联有11年没有周末。 相反，为了提高生产力，公民每七天就被随机分配一天假期。 由于每天都有 80% 的人口在工作，工厂永远不需要停电。

新工作日历实施后不久，一名心怀不满的工人写给《真理报》的一封信概述了这些问题：“如果我们的妻子在工厂，孩子在学校，没有人可以探望我们，我们在家能做什么呢？” 写信人问道。 “如果你必须独自度过，那就不是假期。” 当孩子上学时，父母发现自己在家，或者当孩子轮班时，孩子们无人看管。 由于没有共同休息日，大家庭聚会变得不可能。 劳动力变得士气低落、无精打采，预期的生产率飙升从未实现，该政策首先被修改，然后被完全放弃。

不过十一年了。 那不是绝对狂野吗？ 没有周末的世界感觉是不可能的。 一个没有周六夜狂热、没有躁狂星期一的世界。 周日我们可能不再去教堂，但周末我们仍然做礼拜。 朴茨茅斯大学社会和文化史教授布拉德·比文表示：“周末之所以显得重要，是因为它代表了集体时间对市场时间的胜利。” “这不仅仅是休息，而是从工业时钟中夺回自主权。”

星期六和星期日是劳动人民的尊严和人性的神圣之地，充满了神话和仪式。 从西拉·布莱克 (Cilla Black) 到加里·莱因克尔 (Gary Lineker)，我们周末的主角成为了文化的巨人。 我们把周末浪漫化，甚至包括那些平淡无奇的片段——远处割草机的轰鸣声、收音机里传来的分类足球比赛结果的嘎嘎声。 每个人都知道周末意味着什么。 周五下午 4 点 58 分，笔记本电脑盖被折断。 回家路上第一品脱玻璃杯的叮当声和薯条的味道。 周末人行道的慢动作，齿轮从喧嚣变为蜿蜒。 当然，随着时间的推移，这些仪式也发生了变化，周六早午餐时观察行人现在已经成为一种传统，就像周日在家烤肉一样。 随着你经历人生阶段，周末的形状也会发生变化，但在每次迭代中，它仍然是你和同龄人之间的共同经历。

伦敦大学伯贝克学院经济学教授、《星期五是新星期六》一书的作者佩德罗·戈麦斯笑着说：“我 20 岁时度过的周末与现在 40 岁时和孩子们度过的周末非常不同。” “年轻的时候，你会和朋友在一起，而当你老了，你可能会和家人在一起。 最终，你可能会和孙子在一起。 在我们的一生中，我们会经历周末的不同表现。”

但现在很难确定周末从哪里开始和结束。 周五在家工作洗衣服，但周日回复电子邮件。 在经历了艰难的周三和周六的郊游之后，在手机上尽情购物可能会成为一种振奋人心的享受。 传统的周六下午 3 点足球比赛的开球时间已经在电视节目表中一直延续到周一晚上。 理查德·尼克松 (Richard Nixon) 于 1956 年首次预测，每周工作四天的做法在荷兰已成为现实，人们平均工作 32.1 小时。 周五正在悄然脱离工作周，没有人签署文件。 这就提出了一个问题：2026 年的“周末”到底是什么？

值得注意的是，我们所知道的周末概念只有 100 年的历史。 1926 年，亨利·福特改变了工作周的形式，宣布他工厂的工人现在将每天工作 5 小时，而不是 6 小时，而且工资不会减少。 福特并没有发明周末——这个想法在工会、宗教团体和进步雇主的运动中已经酝酿了一个世纪——但通过他在工业界的巨大影响力的支持，两天的自由诞生了。

1926 年 10 月，福特在公司的《福特新闻》中写道：“现在是时候摆脱这样一种观念了，即工人的休闲要么是浪费时间，要么是阶级特权。” 福特的创新在一定程度上是对他早期发明的回应：装配线提高了生产率，但也让工人精疲力尽，工厂缺勤率高达 10%；他在文章中并没有掩饰其中涉及自身利益。 “有更多闲暇的人们需要更多的交通工具，”他继续说道。 一日游的新时尚是销售汽车的有效营销手段。 与此同时，尽管工时减少，他的工厂仍保持稳定的生产力水平。 1938年，面对大萧条时期失业率上升，美国正式采用五天工作周。

在大西洋的这一边，化学家布茨是先驱。 1933 年，公司在诺丁汉开设了一家新工厂，事实证明该工厂效率极高，很快就出现了库存过剩。 由于失业率高达 25%，约翰·布特 (John Boot) 不愿裁员，因此结束了周六早班，在不削减工资的情况下减少了 5,000 名员工的工作时间。 它在商业上取得了成功，导致旷工率降低，并于 1934 年被采纳为 Boots 政策。 由演员埃迪的曾祖父理查德·雷德梅恩（Richard Redmayne）领导的一项政府调查发表了一份“对每周五天的实验性工作的回顾”，其中指出“由于长周末休息和放松的生理和心理影响，员工的耐力和活力得到了改善”。 慢慢地，周末的势头逐渐增强。 在英国，“20 世纪初的周末通常被认为是周六和周日休息半天，”比文说。 “完整的两天周末直到第二次世界大战后才真正被广泛采用。”

在工业化之前，几乎没有连续几天休闲的概念，因为动物和农作物不能被忽视这么久。 工作取决于天气和季节，时钟比太阳更重要。 工厂用哨子和手表改变了时间的运作方式。 轮班和发薪日的机械化鼓声淹没了季节和圣日的旧节奏。

随着工作的组织变得更加严格，休闲也可能变得更加严格。 休假不仅是对工人的让步，也是消费资本主义的引擎。 有周末的人们会去体育场馆，购买野餐篮和新衣服，需要电影票。 到了 20 世纪末，随着廉价航班的到来，这已经演变成迷你休息：一个微型假期，旨在适应周末。 曾经与经济相反的休闲时间，如今已成为经济的一部分。

几代人以来，英国的周末都​​围绕着一个不可改变的约定：周六下午 3 点开球。 “周末是关于休息的，但也是关于激情的，”戈麦斯说。 “我们大多数人都没有足够的运气对我们的工作充满热情，但在周末我们可以追随我们的热情。” 足球和一周中最好的一天之间的联系是国民对这项运动的热爱的本质。 部分原因可能是足球象征着周末最美好的时光，所以我们最终对它如此着迷。

道德——以及道德的缺失——一直是周末的主题。 当星期天（礼拜时间）是唯一的休息日时，技术工人养成了将空闲时间延长到“圣星期一”的习惯，即在特别热情的饮酒一天后不再去上班。 雇主允许周六下午休息，然后是一整天，部分原因是希望将宿醉时间提前一天。 维多利亚时代的改革者沉迷于酗酒，希望免费的周六能够鼓励体面的娱乐活动：有组织的运动、园艺、家庭郊游。 福特是禁酒令的坚定支持者，他认为饮酒的非法性使他的两天周末之旅变得安全。 （“休息一天不再是醉酒一天，”他说。）

现实从未如此清晰。 周末既调皮又美好，既是坏行为，也是周日最好的。 这些日子适合挥霍购物、狂欢饮酒和勾搭，但也适合忏悔，无论是公园跑步、DIY 还是实际祈祷。 不过，祈祷的意义或许不大：根据国家社会研究中心的数据，1900 年，大约三分之一的英国人定期去教堂；现在，这个数字约为二十分之一。 故事中的两个时刻非常突出，说明星期日如何失去了作为一个日子的特殊地位，如果不是崇拜的话，那就是具有更高目的的日子。 1994年，《星期日营业法》允许英格兰和威尔士的大型商店在星期日营业。 然后，四分之一个世纪后，大流行的封锁打破了教堂与其社区之间现在脆弱的联系，并使许多年长的教区居民对聚集在通风不良的教堂保持警惕，这可能对健康有害，即使对灵魂有益。

已故的伟大的玛吉·史密斯，正如她经常做的那样，拥有最好的台词。 “什么是周末？” 在《唐顿庄园》中，她带着一位伯爵夫人的困惑问道，她的收入从出生起就用银子舀着吃，而不是在周五晚上用棕色信封发放。 周末是由别人对你的时间的所有权而划分出来的，并且与你的时间所有权存在紧张关系。 更何况对于贵族来说，从生火到扣衣扣，都有仆人做事，每天都是闲暇的一天。 周末感觉像是文明和民主的基石，因为对于那些一周大部分时间都在听从命令而不是下达命令的人来说，周末最重要。

如今，楼上楼下的划分是混合型员工和那些永远无法远程完成工作的员工之间的。 轮班工作和白领工作的相对灵活性之间由来已久的分歧已经加深。 哥本哈根咨询公司 Future Navigator 的创始合伙人 Liselotte Lyngsø 等思想家认为，劳动力正在分裂为“时间所有者”（越来越多地选择工作地点和时间的知识型员工）和“时间奴隶”，后者的工作（如医疗保健、轮班工作或亚马逊或 Deliveroo 驾驶等零工经济角色）仍然顽固地与时钟联系在一起。

对于“时间所有者”来说，星期五正在迅速变成现代的圣星期一。 对于远程工作者来说，工作周的最后一天已经成为一个越来越公开的秘密：日历在技术上是开放的，但大脑和笔记本电脑大多处于待机状态。 2023 年，戈麦斯在葡萄牙进行了为期六个月、每周工作四天的试验，涉及超过 41 家公营和私营公司，“无法减少工作时间的组织——例如托儿所——实行轮班工作，每周休息一天不同。 其他公司决定取消周五的活动。 每当他们的工作日休息时，我们发现许多员工对待这一天的方式略有不同，利用它来完成“生活管理”，以便他们可以在周六和周日自由活动。 周末不仅仅是小时数，它也是社区联系的协调工具。”

与圣星期一一样，“斯基夫日星期五”在英国已被证明是人们顽固地（尽管是默默地）遵守的。 2024 年，伦敦交通局进行了为期三个月的试验，明确取消周五的高峰票价，以吸引通勤者返回伦敦市中心。 但它失败了，尽管有折扣，周五仍然保持安静。 对于笔记本电脑课程来说，周五的内容发生了变化。 包括 LNER 和 Avanti 在内的几家主要铁路公司现在已将周五定为像周六和周日一样完全非高峰的一天，并承认周末对许多人来说开始得更早。

但值得注意的是，对于这些员工来说，周六和周日本身就不断受到工作电子邮件和智能手机时代工作时间之外的联系的任务蔓延的围攻。 “这是同一枚硬币的两面，”戈麦斯说。 工作强度加大，周末时间延长以吸收压力。 “沟通的速度意味着我们现在生活在不断的干扰中，很难找到深度工作或真正休息的空间。 然而，我们仍然以与 100 年前大致相同的方式安排工作周。 这不起作用也就不足为奇了。”

因此，为什么建议将为期三天的周末作为平衡收支的一种方式。 但这都是废话吗？ 这是一个天上掉馅饼的想法，是由不再懂得努力工作意义的懒惰劳动力所梦想的吗？ 绿党支持“迈向”四天工作周，但其他政界人士则持谨慎态度。 2025年，自由民主党领导的南剑桥郡议会已连续两年实行每周四天工作制，遭到时任地方政府秘书史蒂夫·里德的攻击，他表示地方政府“不应该为兼职工作支付全职工资”。 今年 4 月，詹姆斯·克莱弗利 (James Cleverly) 宣布，未来的保守党政府将禁止议会工作人员每周工作四天，并谴责“英国政坛中左翼推动”每周工作四天的做法“完全错误”。

领导英国变革的“四天周基金会”表示，在 61 家报名参加“四天周”试点计划的公司中，有 56 家决定在该计划结束后继续坚持下去。 他们表示，在试验期间，收入平均增加了 35%，员工离职率平均下降了 57%。 英国目前有 260 家公司正式签署了为期四天的工作周。

时间共享者和时间奴隶之间的鸿沟——那些每周工作五天、每周四天或更临时、不太适合周末的轮班工作的人——是有问题的，因为周末是为了共享而设计的。 这是英国文化学会聚集、集体体验的地方。 每一代人都有自己共同的仪式。 婴儿潮一代喜欢周六晚上的电影，X 一代痴迷于周日午餐，千禧一代喜欢涌向农贸市场，而 Z 一代则出于某种原因排队购买在 TikTok 上疯传的烘焙食品。 即使周日的恐怖事件也变得容易处理，因为知道每个人都有同样的感觉。 随着时间所有者和时间奴隶之间、继承的财富和日益杂乱的工资管道之间的鸿沟不断扩大，周末开始感觉不再像一种经历，而更像是一种怀旧的记忆。

有趣的是，技术最初拓展了我们的视野。 铁路让普通人可以到达沿海地区；大规模生产使自行车和汽车变得买得起。 直到最近，技术才突变为今天的能源吸血鬼，吸走了周末的生活。

直到最近十年，在线自传才成为每个人的无偿副业，因此您的朋友在您与他们共进早午餐之前就已经看到了您的度假照片。 我们的友谊转移到了网上，这是一个非常现代的现象，本周的男孩戏剧或家庭争吵已经在文本泡沫和语音笔记中进行了详细的辩论，而无需在酒吧见面。 再加上疫情后“软承诺”的常态化，其中制定计划和取消计划已成为同一个社交仪式的两个部分，而“我看看我的感受”已成为可接受的回复，我们已经变得不太擅长周末的核心要素，即与其他人见面。

或许我们不应该太担心。 自从我们发明了周末以来，我们就一直在焦急地把握住它的脉搏。 维多利亚时代的人担心工人们会浪费宝贵的闲暇时间喝酒。 二十世纪中叶的英国担心电视会让家人呆在家里。 今天的问题是我们周六刷 Instagram，周日回复电子邮件。 仪式发生变化；周末被毁掉的怀疑依然存在。 然而周末依然存在，也许是因为它从来不要求完美。 睡懒觉和熬夜都是同样有效的抵抗形式。 它最神圣的仪式——油腻的煎锅、足球场、周六晚上闪亮的地板电视——都非常不精致。 周末的美好时光仍然胜过品味。

苏联人发现，除非其他人也休息，否则休息一天并没有多大用处。福特明白，工人们需要时间来重新做回自己，即使他希望他们用这段时间购买汽车。 100 岁的时候，为期两天的周末已经到了边缘，渗透到周五，并被周日晚上的电子邮件蚕食。 周末会不断变化，因为工作不断变化。 但它仍然永远是工作发明的最好的东西。
